1.sense: The surah opens on a man's hands and then on the man himself. The hands come first because hands are what a person acts with, and this man's actions against the message are what the surah is about.

notes.t: Abu Lahab was Abd al-Uzza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, an uncle of the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Lahab, father of flame, was a nickname given for his colouring, and the surah uses the nickname rather than the name he was given, which carried the name of an idol inside it.
notes.src: the identification is agreed in the sira and the tafsir; the reason for the nickname is reported in more than one form

notes.t: The reports say the Prophet ﷺ climbed as-Safa and called the clans of Quraysh by name, asked whether they would believe him if he said an army was coming from behind the hill, and was told they had never known him to lie. He then warned them of a punishment, and Abu Lahab said may you perish, is this what you gathered us for.
notes.src: Bukhari, in the Book of Tafsir on Surat ash-Shuʿara and on this surah, and Muslim in the Book of Faith, from Ibn Abbas

notes.t: The opening words are his own words handed back to him. He said may you perish, and the surah returns the sentence with the grammar changed from a wish into a report of what has happened.

links.why: and warn your nearest kin, the command that produced the gathering on as-Safa
another Meccan opponent described in detail and left unnamed

2.sense: The two things a man of his standing would lean on are named and dismissed in one line: what he was given and what he made for himself. Neither did anything for him.

notes.t: The verb is in the past tense about an outcome still in the future. Arabic uses the perfect this way for something certain enough to be reported as already done.
And what he earned is read by some of the early exegetes as his children, on the ground that a man's child counts among his earnings. Others take it as his profits and his standing among his people.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both, and reports the reading as children from more than one of the early exegetes

notes.t: Aghna is from the root of needing nothing, the same root as istaghna. Wealth is exactly the thing that makes a man feel he needs nobody, and this verse tests it and reports the result.

links.why: his wealth will not avail him when he falls
my wealth has not availed me, said on the Day itself

3.sense: The sentence turns to the future and the nickname comes back, this time as a property of the fire. The father of flame is put into a fire that has flame, and the surah does not stop to point out the match.

notes.t: Lahab is the visible flame, the part of a fire that leaps, as distinct from the coals underneath. It appears in verse one as half of his name and here as a quality of the fire, and that repetition is the whole of the wordplay.
Sa-yasla uses the particle sa, which in Arabic points at something coming soon rather than eventually. The surah was recited in Mecca while the man was alive and in good health.

A surah that names a living opponent and states how he will end is a standing risk taken in public. Abu Lahab could have unsettled it by professing belief for an hour, and he did not, and the surah went on being recited in his hearing.

links.why: a fire that only the most wretched will enter, the one who denied and turned away
the fire of Allah, kindled, that rises over the hearts

4.sense: His wife is joined to him in the sentence, and she is named by an act rather than by her name. She carried firewood, and the surah leaves the reader to work out what it was for.

notes.t: Hammalat al-hatab is read literally, that she carried thorn bushes and scattered them where the Prophet ﷺ walked, and idiomatically, since carrying firewood is an Arabic figure for spreading talk between people, because a talebearer feeds a fire. Both readings are old.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir record both the literal and the idiomatic reading

notes.t: She was Umm Jamil, a sister of Abu Sufyan, and the accounts of her hostility are preserved in the biographical literature and in the commentaries, in varying forms.
notes.src: the identification is standard in the sira and the tafsir; the individual incidents are reported with differing wordings

notes.t: The intensive form hammala means one who carries habitually or in quantity, not one who carried once. The word describes a practice rather than an occasion.

links.why: woe to every slanderer and fault finder
the prohibition of slander and backbiting stated as law

5.sense: The last image is a rope around a neck. The word for neck here is the one Arabic poetry uses for the neck a necklace is worn on, and what she has on hers is a hauling rope of twisted palm fibre.

notes.t: Jid is not the plain word for neck, which is unuq. Jid is the neck considered as the place an ornament sits, and the surah puts a working rope exactly where the jewellery would go.
Masad is read as palm fibre twisted into rope, as a rope of iron, and as a chain in the Fire. The lexical sense underneath all three is anything tightly twisted together.
notes.src: at-Tabari and the lexicographers record the several senses without choosing one

notes.t: The surah opens with two hands and closes with a neck, and both are ordinary body parts doing ordinary work. It never describes the size of the Fire or its heat. It describes a woman carrying a load with a rope, which is what she was already doing.

links.why: seize him and put him in a chain of seventy cubits
chains and shackles and a blaze prepared for the deniers
